title: Anger (Shabbat 105b)
hookLine: the Talmud likens anger to idol worship

lines: A DOOR SLAMMED, A PLATE DROPPED.
cards: A cupboard door slammed hard enough to bounce back open. A phone thrown onto the couch. A plate set down a little too loudly, and everyone at the table goes quiet.
Sometimes anger reaches the hands before it reaches the words. A page of the Talmud lists exactly that kind of moment: tearing your clothes, breaking your dishes, flinging your money.
Then it reaches for a startling comparison.

teach.b: Ka'as. Anger. Turn it four ways.
First, the passage. In tractate Shabbat, the Talmud says one who tears his garments in anger, breaks his vessels in anger, or scatters his money in anger should be seen as one who worships idols.
Idolatry, in Jewish thought, is a grave charge. Why would a smashed plate earn it? Second, the reason.

That's how the evil inclination works, the Talmud says: today it tells you, do this; tomorrow, do that; until it tells you, go worship idols, and you go. Anger is practice in obeying a voice that isn't yours.
Each small surrender trains the next. Third, the verse.

A psalm says: "There shall no strange god be in thee." The rabbis ask what strange god could live inside a person's body, and answer: the evil inclination. Read that way, the idol isn't a statue in a faraway temple.
It's whatever takes the throne inside you for the length of a rage. Fourth, the ordinary Tuesday. Rabbi Eliezer says, in Pirkei Avot: don't be quick to anger.
Not never angry. Slow. Mussar teachers build on that: the space between feeling the heat and acting on it is where you decide who sits on the throne.
Anger may be justified. The worry is the moment it starts giving the orders. A breath before the door slams is a small act of loyalty to who you mean to be.

how: Jews study the Talmud's teaching in Shabbat 105b and Avot's counsel to be slow to anger; Mussar groups often take anger as a trait to work on, practicing a pause before reacting.

o: anger, which can take over who's in charge
a sad mood that comes after a loss
fear of being punished for a sin

s: the Talmud says any feeling of anger is idolatry
it names acting out: tearing clothes, breaking dishes, flinging money in anger.
the Talmud explains it by the evil inclination's habits
today it says do this, tomorrow do that, until it says worship idols.
Avot says never to be angry
Rabbi Eliezer's line is don't be quick to anger: slow, not never.

games.q: someone wrecks your plans and you want to throw your phone across the room. according to Shabbat 105b, why does it matter?
o: because each surrender trains you to obey a voice not your own.
games.why: the Talmud says the evil inclination works step by step: today this, tomorrow that, until it says worship idols.

practice: Bring up something mid-sized that made you angry lately, let a little of the heat return, and notice where it lives: jaw, chest, hands.
Notice the words it wants to send, and don't send them; watch the anger like weather from a window, breathing slowly, and ask what you'd say if you answered tomorrow instead.
If you pray, you can ask in your own words to be slow to anger.

wordCard.voice: Ka'as. Anger. The Talmud compares acting out in anger to serving a strange god, because for that moment, something else is in command. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: anger, vexation; the word the Talmud uses in Shabbat 105b.

carryVoice: Your line: anger is idolatry. The tradition asks for slow anger, not for no feelings at all. Breathe easy tonight.

sources.q: There shall no strange god be in thee
